title: Good Ayis Are Always on the Job — What a Domestic-Help Consultant Really Sells Isn't Information
dek: Domestic help is a supply-led industry: good ayis never reach the open market, and the consultant's hard part isn't closing the deal but handling replacements after the sale; both employers and ayis are just pass-throughs for their wages.
why: A frontline Gen-Z domestic-help consultant lays out a neglected essential industry: matching mechanics, pricing, off-platform deals, boundaries — high information density, and the second half is worth more.
who: Dual-income families hiring or about to hire a yuesao or yuer sao, and founders and investors watching domestic help and local life services.
skip: From 1:35:37, the part about the twins family interviewing over picture books is more story than substance — feel free to fast-forward.

points.h: Good ayis are always on the job
points.body: This market has a circulation paradox: highly rated ayis never reach the open market. She works for one family for two or three years, and the moment she leaves she's referred straight to the next one. The ones actually circulating on the market are usually the ones nobody could settle on. So the industry's core contradiction is supply — where good ayis come from and how they get discovered. A domestic-help company is essentially a human resources company: it has to recruit, train and re-match.

points.h: Every woman in this trade has a story
points.body: The ayi profile clusters in tier-three and tier-four cities or even poor villages, aged 30 to 45, many divorced or single. Live-in sisters spend little time with their own families, giving their time to another family instead. Two clear traits mark their choice of this work: they like children, and they hunger to earn — not to sit comfortably in the village farming and drinking tea, but to pack up everything they own, buy a green-skin train ticket and squeeze their way to Shanghai.

There has to be a sense of boundaries and tact between ayi and employer — not just for the ayi, but for the employer too. Some people spoil the ayi past the line, but everyone takes a mile when given an inch. More subtly, a live-in ayi is together with the family 24 hours a day and may know more about the household's private life than close relatives do — that's a lot of pressure. Some moms are doing widowed-style parenting with the dad absent, and it's the ayi who keeps the mom company longer; the two become teammates.

points.h: Employers and ayis are both pass-throughs for their wages
points.body: For the employer it's like being a pass-through for wages, and the same goes for the ayi: the monthly WeChat transfer comes in, and immediately two kids' tuition goes out, then the household living expenses, transferred straight away. For many yuesao and yuer sao, their income is the most important or even the only source for the family, which is why her role as wife within the family structure is so dominant. That also explains why employers care about the ayi's family background — you're not hiring a company employee, and her stability is directly tied to her family situation.

points.h: How ten pages of job requirements don't scare the ayi off
points.body: The longest yuesao job spec I've seen ran a full ten pages, yet the price was just the market average. Employers think that if they write out every minute and second, the ayi will execute like a robot — but people are emotional. The consultant won't forward it directly; instead she starts with a voice call to set the ground: asking about luggage, giving directions, telling her the client says just arrive at this time, then explaining that company rules require the employer to list requirements and she can come to me anytime with questions. That way the ayi feels she's been handed a guidebook, not interrogated.

points.h: Signing isn't hard — replacing someone is the test
points.body: Yuesao jobs are booked in advance; yuer sao jobs are mostly urgent — an ayi can only enter the market once she leaves her previous family, so demand is pressing. Many employers assume that whoever is urgently available must be bad, when in fact it's often the booked one who's the fake. Signing a client isn't hard for a consultant: as long as the employer has a need and a budget, someone can always be found. The real difficulty is long-term after-sales — you can be thrilled in the interview and still, with some probability, sour on it later, and replacing someone is what truly tests a consultant's level.

points.h: The hardest case requires reading the family's core relationship
points.body: The hardest case: a single-mother female executive who wanted a daytime child development companion, but also expected this person to do housework to cleaning-level standards — while the companion's hourly rate is twice a cleaner's. The consultant dealt with the assistant, and the core need was also shaped by the executive's mother. The compromise was cleaners for cleaning and companions for companionship, but the mother still had to be won over. The person finally found was the polar opposite of the original spec — originally under 35 with a bilingual kindergarten teaching background; in the end, a sister approaching 50 with an education background and live-in experience.

points.h: Yuesao start at 15k, yuer sao depend on age
points.body: In tier-one cities a yuesao's 26-day contract price is generally 15,000–16,000 or more; for one with two or three years' experience who has genuinely cared for newborns, it's basically 15,000 to 20,000. Shanghai rates for yuer sao: beginners from 7,000, experienced hands depending on age, skills and work history basically 8,000-plus; stack on English, bilingual, early education or driving and it's 10,000-plus. Prices have risen in recent years partly because higher-educated people are entering the trade, and partly because supply still falls short of demand.

points.h: Consensus and trade norms are what this industry lacks most
points.body: The live-in norm is that the ayi brings her own personal items and the employer provides big items like bedding, but the two sides haven't formed a consensus yet. Some think it's lovely when an ayi who's been there a long time grows attached and spends her own wages buying things for the baby; others find it too close. A common situation is a mother who's unhappy that the child is too attached to the ayi. Consultant training teaches this: the person in a family who should have the closest contact is the mom — not the dad, and not the grandparents.

points.h: Young people doing domestic work is long past being a meme
points.body: By the time something becomes a meme, the number of people doing it is already beyond what you'd imagine. The contraction of the tutoring industry fed a lot of talent into domestic help; child development companions are very young, a cohort in their twenties, because jobs are hard to find and this trade provides room and board and responsibility for just one child. After five to eight years of live-in experience, yuying shi and yuesao get too old to keep up with the kids and shift toward training-instructor roles. But whether you do yuying shi or child development companion, it's very hard to build a three-to-five-year career plan.

quotes.text: For the employer it's like being a pass-through for wages, and for many ayis it's really the same.
Because an ayi is a person — people aren't machines, people are in a state where they have emotions.

Signing a client isn't a hard thing for us — we can always help the employer find someone they're satisfied with, as long as they have a need, right, and a budget. But the hard part usually comes later.
I think right now both sides of the employment relationship haven't really formed this consensus, haven't yet accumulated that process of understanding roughly what state this industry is in.
When something has already become a meme, the number of people doing it is already beyond your imagination.
